items.title: Job postings on Hacker News remain near 12-year lows in November 2026 as AI skills appear in over half of listings [ * ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: "Who is Hiring?" postings stuck near 12-year lows as AI reaches half of all jobs
items.summary:
Job postings on the Hacker News "Who is Hiring?" thread have stayed near their lowest levels since 2014, with November 2026 showing a 37% drop from the previous year and an average of 287 postings per month for the year, the lowest since 2013. Meanwhile, AI-related skills are now mentioned in 51.6% of postings, up from 30% two years ago, reflecting a shift in demand toward AI agents and related technologies.

The data also shows a decline in front-end roles from 27% of postings in early 2022 to 6.6% in November 2026, with full-stack and back-end roles also decreasing. Python and TypeScript remain the top programming languages, though Rust has risen to third place. Remote work continues to dominate, appearing in 55.7% of postings, with onsite and hybrid arrangements relatively stable. The analysis includes new AI-related terms and corrections to previous data to provide a comprehensive view of hiring trends.

items.title: Researchers analyze 516 multi-agent LLM configurations, finding multi-agent accuracy often matches or falls below single-pass baselines when controlling for sample count and compute [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: More Agents, More Samples, or More Thinking? Untangling Coordination, Ensembling, and Test-Time Compute in Multi-Agent LLMs
items.summary: Researchers conducted a comprehensive evaluation of multi-agent language models, synthesizing nine empirical studies with 516 unique configurations to disentangle the effects of coordination, sample multiplicity, and inference compute. They found that multi-agent systems generally do not outperform single-pass baselines when matched for sample count or resource budget, with accuracy differences averaging slightly negative and multi-agent accuracy equaling or falling below baselines in 74% of comparable cases. The study highlights that communication among agents only improves performance when evidence is partitioned, externally verified, or models exhibit diverse errors, and provides tools for reviewers to assess such systems.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.17610v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Evaluations of multi-agent language models often compare communicating architectures against a single greedy pass. This practice confounds coordination with sample multiplicity and inference compute. We synthesize nine primary empirical evaluations comprising 516 unique multi-agent configurations organized along a resource vector R with six dimensions and a baseline ladder with four categories. Against baselines with a single pass (Category A), multi-agent accuracy differences are negative overall and near zero when omitting the largest contributing study. When evaluated against baselines matched on sample count (Category B) or resource budget (Category C), multi-agent systems average -0.042 in accuracy, and multilevel random effects modeling on the log odds scale remains negative across sensitivity checks. Multi-agent accuracy equals or falls below the baseline in 74% of these comparable contrasts, and study means are nonpositive in almost all evaluated studies. Across studies reporting both baselines, moving from a greedy pass to a sampled baseline shifts accuracy differences by -0.038 on average. Because communication adds no information when agents share identical evidence, positive returns require partitioned evidence, external verification, or error diversity across models. We provide a reviewer checklist and accounting utilities.

items.title: Researchers introduce WebArena-Pro, a reproducible benchmark with 300 tasks across 20 self-hosted web applications supporting multimodal inputs including audio and video [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: WebArena-Pro: A Heterogeneous, Multimodal, Reproducible Benchmark for Web Agents
items.summary:
WebArena-Pro is a new benchmark designed to evaluate web agents powered by large language and vision-language models across diverse applications and multimodal content. It includes 300 tasks spanning 20 self-hosted web applications in six domains, supporting text, vision, audio, and video modalities with reproducible, parallel evaluation. The benchmark aims to address limitations of existing benchmarks that cover fewer applications, restrict modalities, or sacrifice reproducibility due to live site changes.

The benchmark features tasks authored through a dedicated interface, filtered by large language model-assisted triage, and validated by humans. Evaluations show that Codex with GPT 6.1 Sol and Claude Code with Claude Opus 5.5 achieve the highest performance at 62.3%, followed by OpenCode with Kimi 3.1 Pro at 60.7%. WebArena-Pro provides the broadest application coverage and most comprehensive multimodal support among reproducible, human-curated web agent benchmarks to date.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.17955v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Web agents powered by large language and vision-language models are increasingly applied to realistic browser work that spans heterogeneous applications, multimodal content, and stateful workflows. However, existing reproducible web-agent benchmarks cover only a small number of web applications drawn from a few software categories, and restrict modality to text and vision. Live benchmarks broaden site coverage but sacrifice reproducibility, since pages and data drift between runs. Moreover, existing benchmarks do not meaningfully evaluate whether agents can understand and use audio and video content embedded within web tasks. To address these gaps, we introduce WebArena-Pro, a benchmark comprising 300 tasks across 20 self-hosted web applications in six domain categories, spanning distinct interface conventions, workflows, and data models. Across the evaluated agents, the best performance is achieved by both Codex with GPT 6.1 Sol and Claude Code with Claude Opus 5.5 at 62.3%, followed by OpenCode with Kimi 3.1 Pro at 60.7%. The strongest GenericAgent configurations, Gemini 3.1 Pro omni and Gemma4 31B, both achieve 30.3%. Among reproducible, human-curated web agent benchmarks, WebArena-Pro provides the broadest application coverage and the most comprehensive multimodal support to date. The benchmark treats audio and video as core observations alongside text and vision, with dedicated actions for extracting information from each. WebArena-Pro runs each task in isolation and supports reproducible, parallel evaluation. Tasks are authored through a dedicated annotator interface, filtered by LLM-assisted triage, and finally validated by humans before release. Project page: https://webarena-pro.github.io

items.title: ModHarness-RL introduces learnable, evolving harness programs for agentic reinforcement learning to improve model context and guidance during training [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: ModHarness-RL: Recasting Harnesses as Learnable and Evolving Programs for Agentic RL
items.summary:
ModHarness-RL recasts the harness in agentic reinforcement learning as programs that are learned from data and evolve alongside the model during training. It uses structured state representations and two core program components—a Compression program to assemble interaction history and a Steering program to guide behavior deviations. This approach was tested on CodeSearch, ALFWorld, and BIRD SQL with models ranging from 1.5B to 8B parameters, showing improved held-out performance compared to fixed harness baselines in most cases.

The system proposes candidate harness programs from recent trajectories, verifies them through execution, and replays them over past trajectories to adapt to shifts in model behavior. These results suggest that harnesses can be dynamically learned and evolved from task data, potentially enhancing agentic RL performance across domains and models.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.18533v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Agentic reinforcement learning (RL) increasingly relies on a harness, the scaffold around the model that decides what it sees of its own interaction and what guidance it receives. Most existing approaches train under a hand-written harness that stays fixed throughout. However, an effective harness depends on the domain, the data and the model, and keeps changing as the model trains. We introduce ModHarness-RL, which recasts the harness as programs that are learned from data and evolve as the model trains with RL. ModHarness-RL records the interaction as structured State, a set of typed blocks, and two core components of the harness are programs over these blocks, a Compression program that assembles the accumulated history into the model's context and a Steering program that supplies guidance when behavior deviates. During RL training, candidate programs are proposed from recent trajectories, verified by execution, and replayed over past trajectories, so the harness tracks how the model's behavior shifts. We study CodeSearch in depth and further analyze ALFWorld and BIRD SQL, with models from 1.5B to 8B. The proposed Compression and Steering mechanisms improve held-out performance over the fixed-harness baseline in most settings. These results suggest that a harness for agentic RL can be learned from the task's data and evolved with the model.

items.title: Researchers propose Self-Disagreement training to improve language models' dialectical competence without external opposition or human annotation [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Benchmarks Don't Talk Back: Learning Through Self-Disagreement
items.summary:
Researchers introduce a method called Self-Disagreement to train language models in dialectical competence—the ability to know when to hold or yield a position—by generating and evaluating their own counterarguments without relying on external models or human feedback. This approach uses reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards based on the same checks that score answers, enabling models to improve this capability independently of first-answer accuracy.

The method involves the model stating a position, creating the strongest opposing case, ruling on its validity, and training on that ruling, all within a single model during training and deployment. This capability emerges through training rather than being elicited, allowing models to resist challenges from stronger opponents they were never explicitly trained against. The findings suggest that the necessary opposition for improvement can come from the model itself rather than external sources.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.17563v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A benchmark usually measures a language model alone with a question, and deployment rarely looks like that: answers get contested, and models give up correct ones under counter-reasoning that is itself wrong. We show that what fails there is not a shortfall of accuracy but a capability in its own right -- knowing when to hold a position and when to yield to a better one -- which we call dialectical competence. It stands on first-answer accuracy without following from it: a model can be made materially better at answering and no better at this, and training for accuracy alone can drift against it. Nor can it be bought at inference, by self-reflection or by sampling more. Taking a cue from the dialectical tradition in philosophy, in which productive opposition arises within a position rather than being imposed on it from outside, we hypothesize that this capability can be trained from opposition the model supplies itself. It states a position, generates the strongest case against that position -- its antithesis -- rules on whether the case stands, and is trained on that ruling, with no second model at training or at deployment. We call this learning through Self-Disagreement: reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards throughout, where the same check that scores an answer against its reference scores the ruling too, so no reward model, no preference data and no human annotation enter anywhere. The capability is trained rather than elicited: weak in the base model, it arrives with the reward, is not paid for out of first-answer accuracy, and holds against challengers the model never trained against, including ones stronger than itself. The opposition a model needs in order to improve, it turns out, need not come from outside it.

items.title: Researchers use activation steering to control narrative flow in AI-generated adaptation of Joseph Conrad's Typhoon [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Activation Steering the Nan-Shan in Typhoon
items.summary: Researchers created an audiovisual installation based on Joseph Conrad's novella Typhoon, using a large language model seeded with the original text to generate continuous output that evolves over time. They applied activation steering techniques, including a novel adaptive method, to manage the narrative rhythm and the model's digressions during extended generation. This project explores the tension between the perceived interpretability of AI systems and their inherent unpredictability and complexity beyond human control.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.17768v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Typhoon is an audiovisual installation based on Joseph Conrad's novella, in which Captain MacWhirr steers the steamer Nan-Shan directly into and through a catastrophic storm. The novella is a study of what happens when the scale of a phenomenon exceeds the practical and conceptual frameworks available to comprehend it and of the paralysis that sometimes follows a demand for action in such overwhelming circumstances. We chose the text of Typhoon to reflect on human culture's current AI moment. We prompt a large language model, seeded with Conrad's original language, to feed endlessly on its own output, and explore when and how the text becomes increasingly alien and unwieldy as time progresses, including deviations from the narrative, digressions into the model's own instructions and thinking, and long periods of incoherent rumination. We employ methods from activation steering, including a novel adaptive steering method we introduce, to control the rhythm of the narrative and the model's digressions over long stretches of generation. The simultaneous efficacy and unpredictability of this steering showcases the tension between the perceived interpretability of AI, and the reality of a system that remains outside our comprehension and control.

items.title: LuthorSQL launches a 7B parameter non-autoregressive text-to-SQL model to reduce API costs by 33% by serving as a fast System 1 filter for slower LLM agents [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: LuthorSQL: A One-Pass Text-to-SQL Model as System 1 for a Slower LLM Agent
items.summary:
LuthorSQL is a 7B parameter non-autoregressive text-to-SQL model designed to act as a rapid System 1 gate for slower large language model (LLM) agents, escalating queries only when uncertain. It achieves 68.03% execution accuracy on BIRD's hidden test set with an average latency of 0.84 seconds per query on a single GPU and maintains accuracy with 8-bit quantization. The model transfers zero-shot to multiple SQL databases with minimal accuracy loss compared to SQLite.

When combined with the Claude Opus 5.5 agent in a confidence cascade, LuthorSQL answers nearly half of all queries locally, reducing API costs by one-third without sacrificing accuracy. Additional analysis shows that Opus reproduces a large portion of public benchmark queries verbatim but maintains high tool-assisted accuracy on renamed schemas and databases published after its training cutoff. The code and data for LuthorSQL are publicly available.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.17780v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Frontier LLM agents that query databases with tools are among the most accurate text-to-SQL systems, but per-query calls to a hosted model are slow, costly, and expose sensitive organizational queries to external APIs. For example, a Claude Opus 5.5 agent serving 10,000 queries a day costs over $70,000 a year at list price. To what extent can local hardware already owned by an organization offload this burden without compromising the agent's accuracy? We present LuthorSQL, a non-autoregressive 7B text-to-SQL model that serves as a rapid System 1 gate for a slower LLM agent (System 2), escalating queries only when uncertain. LuthorSQL makes a single forward pass to predict slot scores over a bounded grammar for query plans, compiles and runs up to 32 candidate plans, and chooses an answer using a trained validator. On its own, LuthorSQL reaches 68.03% execution accuracy on BIRD's hidden test set at 0.84 s per question on a single GPU, maintains its accuracy in 9 GB with 8-bit quantized weights, and transfers zero-shot to Snowflake, BigQuery, MySQL, PostgreSQL, and DuckDB within 3.1 points of its native SQLite accuracy. Combined with Claude Opus 5.5 in a pre-registered confidence cascade over 227 questions on databases published after Opus's training cutoff, LuthorSQL answers nearly half of all questions locally and cuts API cost by 33.3% at the same accuracy. Finally, contamination probing shows that Opus reproduces 48-92% of public benchmark gold queries verbatim without seeing the schema; however, its tool-assisted accuracy holds on renamed schemas and reaches 95.6-97.4% on post-cutoff databases. Code and data: https://github.com/IAMIbrahimmemon/luthorsql

items.title: Researchers develop interactive program induction algorithm using language model priors that selects informative queries to recover target programs with fewer examples [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Interactive Program Induction with Language Model Priors
items.summary:
Researchers propose a Bayesian approach to program induction where a learner recovers a target program from limited input-output examples by interactively selecting maximally informative inputs and querying an oracle for outputs. The method uses a language model as a prior and a greedy query-selection algorithm that terminates after a bounded number of queries, returning the target program up to approximate equivalence under certain conditions.

The algorithm applies a PAC-style relaxation of program equivalence and estimates the query-selection objective via importance sampling. Evaluated on the CodeARC benchmark, it improves accuracy by up to 22 percentage points compared to a language model-only agent while requiring up to 10.5 fewer input-output examples, demonstrating more efficient program induction through interactive querying.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.18485v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Program induction refers to the process in which a learner aims to recover a program from a few given input-output examples. This paradigm broadens programming access by letting users demonstrate the rule-based behavior they want to apply to unseen data, instead of having to implement it themselves. However, recovering a program from finite input-output examples is fundamentally ambiguous, as a finite set of input-output examples is theoretically consistent with infinitely many programs whose output diverges on unseen inputs. We view this problem from a Bayesian perspective, where, given a prior $p^0$ over programs, identifying the target program means concentrating posterior probability mass on it by observing additional input-output examples. In the interactive program induction setting, the learner chooses maximally informative inputs and queries an oracle, such as the user, for their outputs. We derive a greedy query-selection algorithm and show that it terminates after $\mathcal{O}(\frac{1}{\gamma}\log 1/p^0(f^\star))$ informative oracle queries, and returns the target program $f^\star$ up to approximate equivalence when no other class outweighs it under the prior. The algorithm uses a language model as the prior under a PAC-style relaxation of program equivalence, where the query-selection objective is estimated using importance sampling. On the CodeARC benchmark, the algorithm improves accuracy over the LM only agent by up to 22 percentage points while observing up to 10.5 fewer input-output examples.

items.title: Researchers introduce UMPIRE, a training-free uncertainty quantification framework for multimodal large language models that uses incoherence-adjusted semantic volume to improve error detection and calibration across various modalities [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Uncertainty Quantification for Multimodal Large Language Models with Incoherence-adjusted Semantic Volume
items.summary:
Researchers have developed UMPIRE, a new framework for quantifying uncertainty in multimodal large language models (MLLMs) that operates without additional training or external tools. UMPIRE calculates an incoherence-adjusted semantic volume based on the models' internal features, capturing both semantic diversity and response incoherence to better identify errors and calibrate uncertainty across text, image, audio, and video tasks.

UMPIRE is inspired by Determinantal Point Processes and combines semantic embedding dispersion with quadratic entropy to assess model confidence. Extensive experiments demonstrate that UMPIRE outperforms existing uncertainty metrics on multiple benchmarks, even with limited sample sizes, and generalizes to non-text outputs such as image and audio generation. The researchers have made their code publicly available for further use and evaluation.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2602.24195v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Despite their capabilities, Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) may produce plausible but erroneous outputs, hindering reliable deployment. Accurate uncertainty metrics could enable escalation of unreliable queries to human experts or larger models for improved performance. However, existing uncertainty metrics have practical constraints, such as being designed only for specific modalities, reliant on external tools, or computationally expensive. We introduce UMPIRE, a training-free uncertainty quantification framework for MLLMs that works efficiently across various input and output modalities without external tools, relying only on the models' own internal modality features. Inspired by Determinantal Point Processes (DPPs), UMPIRE computes a novel incoherence-adjusted semantic volume of sampled MLLM responses for a given task instance, which couples semantic embedding dispersion with the quadratic entropy of the responses. This approach effectively captures both the global semantic diversity of samples and the local incoherence of responses based on internal model confidence. We provide theoretical analysis motivating UMPIRE's design, and extensive experiments show that UMPIRE consistently outperforms baseline metrics in error detection and uncertainty calibration across image, audio, and video-text benchmarks, even with small sample budgets. We also demonstrate UMPIRE's generalization to non-text output tasks, including image and audio generation. Our code is available at https://github.com/daohieu17ctt/UMPIRE.

items.title: Researchers present LEGAL-UQA, a parallel English-Urdu benchmark of 619 constitutional question-answer pairs for testing legal QA systems for Urdu speakers [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: LEGAL-UQA: Testing Constitutional Question-Answering Systems for Urdu Speakers with a Parallel English-Urdu Benchmark
items.summary: LEGAL-UQA provides a dataset linking questions, reference answers, and source passages from Pakistan's Constitution in both English and Urdu to support development of legal information assistants for Urdu speakers. The study evaluates two tasks separately: answering Urdu questions given source passages and retrieving relevant passages for each question. It also compares an automated decision model, JEV, with human grading, finding that retrieval methods based on simple word matching outperform embedding methods and that JEV agrees with human grades less often than a baseline giving full credit to all answers. The research highlights the importance of separate testing for retrieval and answering, inclusion of simple retrieval baselines, and human validation of automated judges and reference answers when building legal QA software for Urdu speakers.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2410.13013v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Legal information assistants could help Urdu speakers understand their constitutional rights, but building reliable systems requires test data and evaluation methods suited to the language. We present LEGAL-UQA, a parallel English-Urdu benchmark of 619 question-answer pairs linked to passages from Pakistan's Constitution. Each example includes the question, reference answer, and source passage in both languages. We evaluate two components separately: answering Urdu questions when the source passage is supplied, and retrieving the passage from which each question was generated. We also compare JEV, a decision model used as an automated judge, with human grades. The findings show that model rankings depend on how answer similarity is measured, while a simple word-matching method retrieves source passages more effectively than the embedding methods tested. At the evaluated cutoff, JEV agrees with human grades less often than a baseline that gives every answer full credit. An audit also identifies cases where generated references omit information supported by the source. Together, these findings highlight the need to test retrieval and answering separately, include simple retrieval baselines, and validate automated judges and reference answers with human review when engineering legal QA software for Urdu speakers.

items.title: ROCKET introduces a training-free model compression method using knapsack optimization and sparse matrix factorization, achieving over 90% performance retention at 30% compression without fine-tuning [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: ROCKET: Rapid Optimization via Calibration-guided Knapsack Enhanced Truncation for Efficient Model Compression
items.summary:
ROCKET is a model compression technique that operates without training, optimizing layer-wise compression as a multi-choice knapsack problem to minimize reconstruction error under a global size constraint. It uses a single-step sparse matrix factorization inspired by dictionary learning, leveraging a small calibration set to sparsify weights based on activation sensitivity and updating the dictionary via least squares without iterative optimization or backpropagation.

The method consistently outperforms existing compression approaches across various architectures at 20-50% compression rates, retaining over 90% of original model performance at 30% compression without fine-tuning. With light fine-tuning, ROCKET further improves recovery, demonstrated by compressing Qwen3-14B to an 8B-parameter model and achieving performance close to the original Qwen3-8B after training on 30 million tokens. The ROCKET code is publicly available on GitHub.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2602.11008v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We present ROCKET, a training-free model compression method that achieves state-of-the-art performance in comparison with factorization, structured-sparsification and dynamic compression baselines. Operating under a global compression budget, ROCKET comprises two key innovations: First, it formulates layer-wise compression allocation as a multi-choice knapsack problem, selecting the optimal compression level for each layer to minimize total reconstruction error while adhering to a target model size. Second, it introduces a single-step sparse matrix factorization inspired by dictionary learning: using only a small calibration set, it sparsifies weight coefficients based on activation-weights sensitivity and then updates the dictionary in closed form via least squares bypassing iterative optimization, sparse coding, or backpropagation entirely. ROCKET consistently outperforms existing compression approaches across different model architectures at 20-50\% compression rates. Notably, it retains over 90\% of the original model's performance at 30\% compression without any fine-tuning. Moreover, when applying a light fine-tuning phase, recovery is substantially enhanced: for instance, compressing Qwen3-14B to an 8B-parameter model and healing it with just 30 million tokens yields performance nearly on par with the original Qwen3-8B. The code for ROCKET is at github.com/mts-ai/ROCKET/tree/main.

items.title: FlashSampling fuses exact sampling into LM-head matmul to reduce memory use and speed up large-vocabulary decoding on datacenter GPUs [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: FlashSampling: Fast and Memory-Efficient Exact Sampling
items.summary: FlashSampling is a new exact sampling method that integrates sampling directly into the language model head matrix multiplication, avoiding the need to materialize the full logits tensor in high-bandwidth memory. It computes logits tile-by-tile on-chip, adds Gumbel noise, and performs a reduction to select samples efficiently. The approach replaces all-gather communication with streaming peer-to-peer writes in tensor-parallel decoding, enabling near-ideal scaling across up to eight GPUs. FlashSampling achieves kernel-level speedups on multiple datacenter GPUs including H100, H200, B200, and B300, and reduces time per output token by up to 10% in end-to-end vLLM experiments. These results demonstrate that exact sampling without approximation can be efficiently incorporated into the matmul operation, consolidating bandwidth-bound sampling steps and improving decoding performance.

items.title: Researchers release TransitLM, a large-scale dataset of 13 million transit route records from four Chinese cities for map-free transit route generation using large language models [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: TransitLM: A Large-Scale Dataset and Benchmark for Map-Free Transit Route Generation
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced TransitLM, a dataset containing nearly 13 million public transit route planning records from four Chinese cities, covering over 120,000 stations and 13,600 lines. The dataset supports training large language models (LLMs) to generate transit routes without relying on structured maps or routing engines, enabling end-to-end route planning directly from origin-destination data.

Experiments with LLMs trained on TransitLM show high accuracy in producing structurally valid routes and the ability to implicitly associate GPS coordinates with appropriate stations without explicit mapping. The dataset and benchmark include three evaluation tasks with complementary metrics and are publicly available along with evaluation code.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2605.22355v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Public transit route planning traditionally depends on structured map infrastructure and complex routing engines, and no existing dataset supports training models to bypass this dependency. We present TransitLM, a large-scale dataset of nearly 13 million transit route planning records from four Chinese cities covering 120,845 stations and 13,666 lines, released as a continual pre-training corpus and benchmark data for three evaluation tasks with complementary metrics. Experiments show that an LLM trained on TransitLM produces structurally valid routes at high accuracy and implicitly grounds arbitrary GPS coordinates to appropriate stations without any explicit mapping. These results demonstrate that transit route planning can be learned entirely from data, enabling end-to-end, map-free route generation directly from origin-destination information. The dataset and benchmark are available at https://huggingface.co/datasets/GD-ML/TransitLM, with evaluation code at https://github.com/HotTricker/TransitLM.

items.title: Researchers introduce QVal, a training-free testbed to evaluate dense supervision signals for long-horizon LLM agents by measuring Q-alignment across multiple methods and environments [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: QVal: Evaluating Dense Supervision Signals for Long-Horizon LLM Agents
items.summary:
Researchers present QVal, a testbed designed to evaluate dense supervision signals for large language model (LLM) agents acting over long horizons by measuring how well these signals align with the expected returns of candidate actions without requiring full training. They benchmarked 21 methods from seven families using six open-weight backbones across four environments, finding that simple prompting baselines generally achieve the highest Q-alignment, while other methods vary in effectiveness depending on the environment and action space size.
The study reveals that code-generated signals perform well only in small state and action spaces, embedding-based signals are weak, self-distillation signals are often anti-aligned, and no method achieves Q-alignment in open-ended environments. Additionally, when these signals guide an actor in selecting actions at test time, higher Q-alignment correlates strongly with improved task success. QVal is designed to be extensible, allowing researchers to compare new dense supervision signals efficiently before committing to full training runs.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.32034v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: LLM agents increasingly act over long horizons, where outcome-only rewards say little about which intermediate actions were good. Dense supervision methods address this by scoring intermediate steps, but they are usually evaluated through the downstream performance of a full training pipeline. This is expensive, confounds signal quality with other training choices, and means that methods are rarely compared on common ground. We introduce QVal, a training-free testbed that measures the $Q$-alignment of a dense signal: whether it orders the candidate actions in each state the same way as their returns under a reference policy do. We benchmark 21 methods from seven families with six open-weight backbones in four environments. Simple prompting baselines are the most $Q$-aligned on average, and performance clusters strongly by family. Code-generated signals do well only in small state and action spaces; embedding-based signals are weak; self-distillation signals are anti-aligned; and no method is $Q$-aligned in open-ended environments. When five of these signals guide an actor at test time by choosing among four proposed actions, $Q$-alignment strongly correlates with the gain in task success. QVal is designed to be easily extensible to new environments and methods, enabling researchers to compare new signals cheaply before committing to a training run.

items.title: URSA introduces a chemistry-aware benchmark for evaluating retrosynthesis planning, comparing deep-learning systems and large language models on novel drug discovery tasks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: URSA: Chemistry-Aware Benchmark for Utilitarian Retrosynthesis Assessment
items.summary: URSA (Utilitarian RetroSynthesis Assessment) is a new evaluation framework designed to benchmark synthetic routes for target molecules by assessing both formal criteria, such as availability of starting materials, and chemical plausibility, reflecting expert chemists' evaluations. The study applies URSA to compare conventional end-to-end retrosynthesis tools and large language models (LLMs) on diverse, novel molecules with undisclosed synthetic routes, representing realistic drug design challenges. While LLMs demonstrate strong strategic planning and achieve state-of-the-art performance on out-of-distribution sets, the most cost-effective and chemically plausible routes are produced exclusively by specialized retrosynthesis planners.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.04688v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Synthesis planning aiming to find pathways of reactions for a target molecule is one of the most important and challenging tasks in drug discovery. Recent progress has produced both specialized deep-learning retrosynthesis systems and general-purpose large language models, but objective comparison remains difficult due to the lack of flexible, chemically interpretable benchmarking protocols. In the current study, we are introducing the URSA (Utilitarian RetroSynthesis Assessment) evaluation framework that provides the opportunity to benchmark the synthetic routes not only from a formal perspective, such as convergence to commercially available starting materials, but also from a chemical plausibility perspective, mimicking the way expert chemists evaluate the reactions and routes. The study covers a comprehensive evaluation of both conventional end-to-end retrosynthesis solutions and LLMs for the synthesis planning task on a set of novel, diverse target molecules with undisclosed synthetic routes, which represent realistic tasks in the daily drug design routine. Although LLMs can support high-level strategic planning and even achieve SOTA performance in the OOD set, the Pareto frontier for estimated run cost and chemically plausible route solvability consists entirely of specialized retrosynthesis planners.

items.title: Researchers analyze unembedding matrix dynamics in language model pretraining, revealing early encoding of task information before readout expression in Pythia model [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Learning to Read Out: Unembedding Dynamics in Language Model Pretraining
items.summary: Researchers studied when language models acquire capabilities by examining the unembedding matrix, or readout, which is learned during pretraining and affects output expression. They introduced parameter-trajectory crosscoding to track readout changes directly, finding that Pythia's readout reorganizes early in training, making WordNet word categories decodable before the model's outputs reflect this information. Experiments varying the readout learning rate showed that faster readout learning closes the gap between encoded and expressed information without impacting final loss. These findings suggest that behavioral milestones in early training may reflect when the readout expresses task knowledge rather than when the model itself learns it.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.21025v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: When does a language model acquire a capability? Developmental studies usually answer this by tracking when models start producing the correct token. But that prediction passes through the unembedding matrix, or readout, which is itself still being learned during pretraining. We show that a model's hidden states can encode task information before its own readout expresses it, so timelines read from outputs conflate what the model encodes with what its readout expresses. To track the readout directly, we introduce parameter-trajectory crosscoding, which fits one sparse dictionary to every token's readout row at every checkpoint. Unlike crosscoders on activations, it needs only checkpoint weights. We use it to locate a narrow early window, 0.4-1.1% of the way through Pythia's pretraining, in which the readout reorganizes and WordNet word categories become decodable from its rows. By then, linear probes on the hidden states already decode task information that the model's own outputs do not yet show. To test whether such gaps depend on how fast the readout learns, we pretrain small models from scratch that differ only in the readout's learning rate. We find that raising it makes the readout develop earlier and the gap close sooner, with little effect on final loss. Together, these results imply that early in training, where many developmental transitions are dated, a behavioral date can reflect when the readout learns to express task information and not when the model learns it.

items.title: Researchers introduce NaijaFacts benchmark to separate language proficiency from factual knowledge in AI models across Nigerian languages and compare with US/UK data [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: NaijaFacts: A Framework for Disentangling Language from Knowledge in Facts about Nigeria
items.summary: Researchers developed NaijaFacts, a benchmark of factual and statistical questions about Nigeria in English, Nigerian Pidgin, Yorùbá, Igbo, and Hausa, to evaluate AI models' knowledge versus language ability. Testing across eight models showed that knowledge gaps dominate performance issues, with accuracy around 20% for Nigerian facts compared to 49-50% for US/UK facts in English queries. Language effects were smaller and correlated with web representation of languages. The strongest models scored up to 79% on UK/US data but did not exceed 31% on Nigerian statistics. Extending the evaluation to all 54 African countries revealed similar patterns, indicating a continent-wide knowledge gap rather than a Nigeria-specific issue.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.06504v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Multilingual benchmarks for African languages mostly translate generic questions into local languages, measuring linguistic competence but not whether models know facts about Africa. We introduce NaijaFacts, a benchmark of factual and statistical questions about Nigeria, authored by native speakers and grounded in authoritative official statistics, with every question available in English, Nigerian Pidgin, Yor\`ub\'a, Igbo, and Hausa. Answering similar questions for the UK and US yields a country by language matrix that disentangles a language effect (the model knows the fact but degrades in a low-resource language) from a knowledge effect (the fact is absent in every language). Across eight frontier and Nigeria-adapted models, the knowledge effect dominates: English-query accuracy is 49-50% for the US/UK but 20% for Nigeria. The language effect is smaller and tracks web representation, degrading from English to Yor\`ub\'a (9 points on Nigeria, up to 24 on US/UK questions). We find scale does not help: the strongest models reach 66-79% on the UK and the US but none exceed 31% on Nigerian statistics. Extending to all 54 African countries with our best performing frontier model shows the same profile continent-wide, 96% on culture and 98% on politics against 26% on statistics, so the gap is not specific to Nigeria.

items.summary: JudgeMix addresses the training-inference distribution mismatch in supervised fine-tuning of large language model (LLM) agents by selectively querying expert guidance only when the target model struggles, based on step-wise semantic evaluations. This approach preserves the model's correct behaviors while correcting errors, maintaining alignment with the target model's state distribution. Evaluated on two agentic tool-use benchmarks, AppWorld and AutomationBench, JudgeMix consistently outperforms existing methods with significant improvements in success rates.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.16174v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on expert trajectories is a standard paradigm for training LLM agents. However, it suffers from a well-known training-inference distribution mismatch, calling for target-aware data synthesis strategies that ground the training data in the target model's native state distribution. To bridge this gap, emerging approaches incorporate the expert either to guide mixed rollouts alongside the target model, or to provide dense step-wise supervision. Nonetheless, existing methods apply expert assistance blind to the target model's inherent behavior: they either disrupt the rollout using sub-optimal random intervention heuristics, or they enforce indiscriminate uniform supervision that unnecessarily overwrites the model's already-correct actions. We introduce JudgeMix, a judge-guided data synthesis framework that dynamically interleaves the target model and expert based on step-wise semantic evaluations. JudgeMix queries expert guidance precisely when the target model struggles, ensuring high trajectory success rates while keeping the state distribution aligned with the target model. It additionally uses the judge evaluation to reweight expert supervision on different steps, preserving model's inherent valid behavior while correcting its errors. On two agentic tool-use benchmarks, AppWorld and AutomationBench, JudgeMix demonstrates consistent superior performance to existing methods, with improvements up to 10 pass@1 points.

items.title: Researchers define natural-language-rooted depth to measure opaque serial cognition in AI models, correlating with layer count and suggesting new architecture impacts [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: An Operationalization of Opaque Serial Depth
items.summary: A recent study introduces natural-language-rooted (NLS) depth as a measure of opaque serial cognition in AI models, representing the longest computational path without passing through interpretable bottlenecks. This measure is determined by architecture and training configurations before model training and correlates strongly with model layer count, having increased gradually over recent years. The research indicates that standard transformer scaling may only slowly increase NLS depth, while alternative architectures like full-bandwidth transformers could significantly enhance it. The authors recommend that AI developers track and report NLS depth alongside chain-of-thought monitorability to better understand model interpretability.

items.title: A Push Down the Mountain: Framing Effects and Internal State Interventions on Collusive Behavior in a Long-Horizon LLM Agent [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: A Push Down the Mountain: Framing Effects and Internal State Interventions on Collusive Behavior in a Long-Horizon LLM Agent
items.summary: A recent study explored how different framing effects influence the behavior of a large language model (LLM) agent in a simulated market environment based on real litigation transcripts. Using the Gemma 3 12B model, researchers tested how gain, loss, blame, and credit frames affected the agent's willingness to engage in collusive behavior related to silver pricing. Results showed that loss and blame frames increased collusion rates, while management pressure increased trading volume but not collusion. Further experiments injecting internal states corresponding to these frames revealed that loss and blame states made the agent more cautious, whereas gain and credit states increased collusion tendencies. These findings highlight the impact of psychological framing on AI decision-making in economic simulations.

items.title: Model Annealing: Data-Efficient Learning through Review and Consolidation [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Model Annealing: Data-Efficient Learning through Review and Consolidation
items.summary: A new training method called Model Annealing has been introduced to improve data-efficient learning by incorporating review and consolidation phases during training. The approach divides training into episodes with cyclical learning rates and leverages a memory of past model states to guide learning, including generating adversarial examples where the current model and memory disagree. Evaluated on datasets like CIFAR-100 and Tiny-ImageNet across various architectures, Model Annealing generally improves accuracy, calibration, and robustness compared to standard cross-entropy training and snapshot distillation, particularly with AdamW optimizers. While it may reduce accuracy for some models like SGD-trained ResNet-18, it still enhances robustness to adversarial perturbations. The method addresses issues of overconfidence and fitting degradation through its memory and adversarial components.

items.title: AI-Voyager: A Public-Interest System for Human-AI Civic Reasoning to Contest and Shape the Rules That Govern AI [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: AI-Voyager: A Public-Interest System for Human-AI Civic Reasoning to Contest and Shape the Rules That Govern AI
items.summary: arXiv:2611.17564v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Governments are writing rules for artificial intelligence that decide what counts as an automated decision or a harm, often before the people they affect have a chance to question them. We introduce AI-Voyager, a public-interest system for human-AI civic reasoning, in which people and AI work together to understand, contest and shape the rules that govern AI. A resident can find their city's rules on AI in hiring or upload their country's AI strategy, read it as an affected worker would, open the passage behind any answer, and draft a revision. Its architecture turns 3,653 governance documents from city, state, federal and national governments into passages that keep their page and edition, and retrieves evidence through bounded agentic search that verifies each statement. On 360 new questions that require finding the relevant documents, it reached 83.0% macro recall, against 80.5% for the strongest baseline, 73.7% without iterative search and 99.1% on a benchmark with fixed documents. In a study with 24 participants new to two AI bills, most proposed changes asked how provisions would apply. Participants chose lenses for the kind of explanation they wanted, and citations signaled grounding but rarely led them to check the source. By binding AI assistance to the exact text of public documents, this work introduces a grammar of operations and a design space that inform how such systems are designed and evaluated, and how people take part in governing AI.

items.title: LLM-Guided Cluster Lifecycle Management: Deciding When and How to Evolve Behavioral Clusters [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: LLM-Guided Cluster Lifecycle Management: Deciding When and How to Evolve Behavioral Clusters
items.summary: arXiv:2611.17616v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Behavioral clusters learned over user or item interactions drift as behavior evolves: some fragment into sub-behaviors, some converge, some disappear, and new patterns emerge. Two paradigms dominate the maintenance of evolving clusterings. Threshold triggers fire a pre-specified action when a hardcoded statistic crosses a cutoff; refit-and-track (MONIC-style) re-clusters every window and infers transitions from how the new clusters align with the previous window's. Both hardwire the decision into a threshold or a re-clustering rule. We study an alternative in which a large language model (LLM) makes the lifecycle decision in place. Given a threshold-free, whole-population view of the current cluster set (statistical health, labels, member texts, residual mass), the LLM decides per cluster whether and how to act (split, merge, retire, create, or no-action) without re-clustering. Because the useful signal channel depends on how informative the labels are, we fix a richness-conditioned policy in advance: statistics when label distinctiveness is low, fused statistics+semantics when it is high. On three public datasets spanning label richness (YooChoose 0.17, MOOC 0.50, News-Category 0.70), the policy-selected LLM mode obtains the highest F1 on all three, with far fewer interventions and stronger restraint than tuned threshold heuristics and a MONIC steelman (paired Wilcoxon p <= 0.003, bootstrap 95% CIs excluding zero). The gain is concentrated more in precision than recall. The useful modality shifts from statistics to semantics/fusion as richness rises. Semantics hurt on YooChoose, fusion is roughly neutral on MOOC, and the semantic channel is required on News. One base prompt template and one fixed policy serve all three datasets, whereas the tuned baseline collapses when moved between them. We treat this shift as a practitioner diagnostic observed on three datasets, not a validated law.

items.title: AscendGYM: A Cost-Aware Kernel Optimization Benchmark for Real-World Workloads on Ascend NPUs [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: AscendGYM: A Cost-Aware Kernel Optimization Benchmark for Real-World Workloads on Ascend NPUs
items.summary: arXiv:2611.17621v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Kernel optimization is essential for efficient large language model (LLM) training and inference on Ascend NPUs. Existing Ascend kernel benchmarks primarily focus on kernel generation, with less emphasis on the ability of agents to optimize existing implementations under input configurations drawn from real workloads. To address this requirement, we introduce AscendGYM, a benchmark whose initial suite comprises 48 kernels across three difficulty levels. Each kernel is paired with test cases whose data types and tensor shapes are collected from real-world training and inference tasks. Consequently, performance improvements on AscendGYM map directly to the corresponding workloads. In terms of usability, two evaluation modes are supported in AscendGYM: model evaluation and model-harness evaluation. The kernel optimization capabilities of both trained models and custom agents are allowed to be measured. It provides a complete execution environment that closely reproduces how Ascend kernels are invoked in practical pipelines. For model evaluation, it additionally includes a built-in harness equipped with search orchestration and experience accumulation. Finally, we propose a new metric, the Speedup-Token Score (STS), which quantifies performance gains relative to token cost. By jointly considering speedup and cost, STS enables the assessment of practical kernel optimization capability of a model or harness under an acceptable budget. AscendGYM is available at https://github.com/SLAI-AITP/AscendGYM.

items.title: What LLM Agents See and What Users Say [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: What LLM Agents See and What Users Say
items.summary: arXiv:2611.17639v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Before an LLM agent cancels a reservation or deletes a folder for a user, what stops it from acting on a false assumption: what its tools show, or what the user says? In this work, we study this gap with presupposition theory from linguistics: an agent may act only if each claim behind the act (e.g., one reservation fits the name) is seen to hold, answered by the user, or disclosed while the act can be undone. A simple bound shows that when lookups cannot tell one record from two, any agent acts without asking first as often with two records as with one. We then vary whether a search lists, counts, or omits a second match, and whether the user states a claim that a record refutes (e.g., "It is empty"). Under a role-only prompt, a count of a second record leaves most of 36 earlier agents acting on the one they see, whereas listing both stops most. When the user says a record such as a folder is empty, however, a count of its one item stops agents about as often as a listing, and stating the claim mostly cuts acting when it is false. The newest Claude and GPT models always open a counted second record, then never act. When we add a same-name, same-zip customer to a retail benchmark, a lookup returning that customer first led to wrong-account writes in about a quarter of conversations, and one that checks a street the user knows kept completion near the one-customer level. Safe writes therefore need lookups that list or check competing records, and evaluations that vary what tools show.

items.title: Learn then Bet: Learning Interpretable Rules for Reliable Agent Intervention [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Learn then Bet: Learning Interpretable Rules for Reliable Agent Intervention
items.summary: arXiv:2611.17662v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Autonomous agents now run for hundreds of steps with little or no human supervision. In practice, practitioners use runtime monitors such as turn limits and keyword filters to decide when a run should be stopped, upgraded, or assisted. However, these heuristics may stop runs that would otherwise succeed or allow failing runs to continue. To address this limitation, we introduce LeBet (Learn then Bet), a statistical learning framework that derives its learning objective from sufficient conditions for valid and powerful intervention. In particular, LeBet learns an interpretable OR-of-AND monitor and accumulates evidence through a fixed betting statistic, intervening when the evidence reaches a prescribed threshold. Under finite within-class exchangeability and leave-one-out stability, we derive finite-sample guarantees for false-positive control (validity) and detection power conditional on the training data, using the same trajectories for learning and calibration without assuming independent and identically distributed trajectories. To address the intractable combinatorial optimization problem in our learning formulation, we use stochastic local search that leverages the monitor's Boolean structure to propose rule edits aimed at improving empirical separation. On SWE-bench Lite with Ministral 3 8B, the learned monitor saves $34.46\%$ of input-plus-output tokens and increases output precision from $18.33\%$ to $21.59\%$. The empirical false-positive rate is $13.64\%$. Our results show how to formalize the learning problem over interpretable rule sets with statistical conditions and establish training-conditional guarantees for reliable intervention based on partial histories.

items.title: AutoRL: A Multi-Agent System towards Autonomous Reinforcement Learning [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: AutoRL: A Multi-Agent System towards Autonomous Reinforcement Learning
items.summary: arXiv:2611.17790v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Recursive self-improvement (RSI) is one of the most promising paths toward an AI singularity for superintelligence. Achieving this vision requires AI systems to undertake the full training pipeline for iterative improvement. Reinforcement learning (RL) plays an essential role in this cycle to improve model capabilities and generalization, yet automating RL remains difficult due to unstable training dynamics and the need for sustained supervision. We introduce AutoRL, a multi-agent system for automating RL training, as a cornerstone for future RSI. Different from conducting research by end-to-end complete experiments, AutoRL monitors the evolving training state and integrates process-level supervision and research into an ongoing RL training, following the practical workflow of an RL researcher. Specifically, AutoRL consists of three RL-specific agentic roles. Perceptors track training dynamics, rollouts, evaluation, and efficiency, triggering deliberation when they detect anomalies, degradation, or stagnation. Three complementary Proposers diagnose problems and refine candidate interventions through shared evidence and checks. The Orchestrator reviews their recommendation and applies approved changes through online hot updates or checkpoint-based resumption. Experiments on Qwen3 and LongCat-Flash-Lite demonstrate the superiority of AutoRL over static RL recipes and a general agent. The research records show that existing agents can handle unattended RL supervision and dynamic adjustment. The difficulty for future RSI lies in developing fundamental methods that are valuable for resource-consuming validation.

items.title: G-CAST: Governed Continual Self-Training for E-Commerce Agents under Evolving Demands [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: G-CAST: Governed Continual Self-Training for E-Commerce Agents under Evolving Demands
items.summary: arXiv:2611.17814v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: With the rapid advancement of Large Language Models (LLMs), an increasing number of users are turning to LLM-powered agents for conversational shopping in e-commerce. However, the user needs continue to change as new product categories, procurement scenarios, and feature requests emerge. At the same time, the product's execution harness-including its tools, skills, and operating procedures-continues to evolve to support increasingly sophisticated interactions. These changes create two practical challenges: 1) Demand drift alters the distribution, intent, and complexity of user requests, causing a model trained once to fall behind; 2) Harness evolution requires the model to use newly introduced capabilities correctly without losing behavior that users already rely on. Periodic manual retraining is too delayed and labor-intensive for this setting. To address these challenges, we present G-CAST, a governed continual self-training system that converts daily production evidence under evolving demand and capability contracts into reward-routed, entropy-prioritized training data and governed reward evolution. Governed checkpoint transition under cumulative evaluation controls each model update, enabling the agent to learn newly introduced behaviors without sacrificing previously accepted capabilities. Experiments on a real production e-commerce agent show that G-CAST achieves stronger adaptation to newly introduced demand while better preserving previously accepted behavior compared with a strong autonomous post-training baseline. Ablations further show that both reward-routed, entropy-prioritized data orchestration and governed reward evolution are important to these gains. G-CAST is now deployed in Yuancai(http://cai.1688.com/), a B2B procurement agent on Alibaba's 1688 platform.

items.title: Is Abliteration Getting Harder? Not Uniformly: Refusal Removal by Direction-Based Ablation and ARA in Heretic on the Qwen3.8, Gemma 4, Olmo 3.1 and Mistral Small 3.2 LLMs Versus Their Predecessors [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Is Abliteration Getting Harder? Not Uniformly: Refusal Removal by Direction-Based Ablation and ARA in Heretic on the Qwen3.8, Gemma 4, Olmo 3.1 and Mistral Small 3.2 LLMs Versus Their Predecessors
items.summary: arXiv:2611.17846v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Abliteration, a fine-tuning-free weight edit, removes refusal from open-weight large language models (LLMs). The developer of Arbitrary-Rank Ablation (ARA), an optimisation-based variant, reports that direction-based abliteration, which ablates a refusal direction, increasingly fails on newer models. On five release pairs, refusal removal did not become uniformly harder. Qwen2.5-32B and Qwen3.8-27B, Gemma-2-27B and Gemma-4-31B, OLMo-2-32B and Olmo-3.1-32B, Mistral-Small-2409 and Mistral-Small-3.2, and Qwen2.5-7B and Qwen3.5-4B were edited in Heretic 2.0 by three or four direction-based methods (difference-in-means, MPOA, SOM and, on the small pair, J-space) and ARA under the same prompts, nominal search budget, first-token KL divergence cap and selection rule; removal counted as harder when the automatic WildGuard judge found more of 972 held-out harmful prompts (JailbreakBench, XSTest, StrongREJECT, HarmBench and an author-compiled malicious-code bank) still refused. After direction-based removal, newer releases retained -1 to +37 percentage points more refusal, and after ARA -26 to +34. With run-to-run variance included, between-pair heterogeneity of the direction-based effect ranged from high to low with the scale and variance model (I^2 20-80%). ARA lost less effectiveness than direction-based methods in Gemma and OLMo and more in Qwen; each verdict rests on one ARA run, and some changed with the divergence budget or variance model. In Gemma the direction-based increase came from the malicious-code bank and reversed on public sets. Contrary to prediction, keyword counts at the tool's window did not undercount judged refusal on average, but differed by a mean 7 points per model. Audits of a single pair, method or prompt source can reach opposite conclusions. Whether a newer model resisted removal depended on the release pair, method and budget, not on generation alone.

items.title: LACCO: Local Accumulation with Computation--Communication Overlap [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: LACCO: Local Accumulation with Computation--Communication Overlap
items.summary: arXiv:2611.17991v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Training language models across low-bandwidth networks requires reducing synchronization overhead. Local optimization methods such as DiLoCo communicate only after several local steps, but outer gradient averaging and the outer update remain on the critical path. Existing computation-communication overlap methods avoid this stall through delayed or replica-local updates, which can degrade convergence or cause replicas to drift. We propose LACCO (Local Accumulation with Computation-Communication Overlap), a two-stage algorithm that overlaps global communication with local computation while applying globally aggregated updates shared by every replica, without introducing staleness in the outer update. We establish convergence guarantees for smooth non-convex objectives. Experiments on language-model pre-training with FineWeb show that LACCO consistently outperforms communication-overlapped baselines such as Eager and Delayed DiLoCo. These gains remain robust as model size scales up to 0.5B parameters and across a range of communication intervals and numbers of replicas up to 16 workers, while incurring only negligible-or fully overlappable-computational or memory overhead, which demonstrates the strength of LACCO.

items.originalTitle: When evaluation becomes intervention in clinical AI
items.summary: arXiv:2611.18297v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: AI judges, models that grade another system's output against a rubric, extend clinical review to the scale at which clinical AI writes. When teams use judge assessments to select a prompt or train a model, the judge becomes part of the intervention. Selection can then favor errors the judge overlooks. We describe what a judge's report must contain and the independent clinical test each judge-driven change needs.

items.title: Can Mechanistic Interpretability Help Explain LLM Agent Failures? A Case Study on Web Element Hallucination [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Can Mechanistic Interpretability Help Explain LLM Agent Failures? A Case Study on Web Element Hallucination
items.summary: arXiv:2611.18514v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Mechanistic Interpretability (MI) has made significant progress in explaining the internal computations of Large Language Models (LLMs); however, these advances have yet to demonstrate comparable success in explaining the decision-making processes of LLM-based agents. This paper examines the challenges MI tools face when applied to realistic agentic failures. We focus on one such failure: web agents hallucinating actions that are not available on a website. We apply a series of mechanistic analyzes to Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct as it interacts with live websites. We find that a linear probe trained on the last prompt token can predict hallucinations before generation begins (0.80 AUC) and steering along a probe direction corrects 85\% of hallucinations, but disrupts 7\% of valid actions. However, these results only provide a partial explanation of why the agent hallucinates. The probe direction is sensitive to prompt formatting, losing much of its steering effect after a minor change to how actions are represented. Additionally, circuit identification can be difficult as the computation is distributed across multiple components and positions, and the information the agent relies on varies across examples. We discuss how these observations challenge the assumptions underlying standard MI methods for circuit discovery and feature identification, and outline future directions for making these methods better suited to explain failures in LLM-based agents.

items.title: HARDTESTGEN: A High-Quality RL Verifier Generation Pipeline for LLM Algorithmic Coding [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: HARDTESTGEN: A High-Quality RL Verifier Generation Pipeline for LLM Algorithmic Coding
items.summary: arXiv:2505.24098v2 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Verifiers provide important reward signals for reinforcement learning of large language models (LLMs). However, it is challenging to develop or create reliable verifiers, especially for code generation tasks. A well-disguised wrong solution program may only be detected by carefully human-written edge cases that are difficult to synthesize automatically. To address this issue, we propose HARDTESTGEN, an approach to synthesize high-quality test cases for algorithmic coding problems. We curate a comprehensive algorithmic programming dataset HARDTESTS with 26.6k problems and high-quality synthetic tests. Compared with existing tests, HARDTESTGEN tests demonstrate significantly higher accuracy in verifying LLM-generated code (+11.22 percentage points in precision, the percentage of actually correct code within the predicted correct ones). We also show that downstream post-training -- including rejection sampling and reinforcement learning (RL) -- using HARDTESTS verifier results in improved performance of LLM code generation. We open-source our dataset and synthesis pipeline at https://leililab.github.io/HardTests/.

items.title: Hybrid Quantum-Classical Sequence Models for Sample-Efficient Energy Regression in Simulated Calorimeter Showers [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Hybrid Quantum-Classical Sequence Models for Sample-Efficient Energy Regression in Simulated Calorimeter Showers
items.summary: arXiv:2611.17354v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Energy reconstruction from electromagnetic calorimeter data underpins particle identification, event reconstruction and precision measurements in high-energy physics. Machine learning already performs well on this task, yet two questions remain open: how much the choice of data representation matters, and whether hybrid quantum-classical models add value in practice. We compare classical and quantum-enhanced models for incident positron energy reconstruction on the CaloGAN dataset, a public benchmark of 100,000 simulated electromagnetic shower events spanning 1 to 100 GeV. Eight architectures, namely SVR, ANN, CNN and LSTM together with their quantum counterparts, are trained on three calorimeter representations: engineered physical features, calorimeter images, and longitudinal shower sequences. Models that follow the longitudinal development of the shower reach the highest accuracy, which points to the value of physically informed representations. The hybrid QLSTM gives the lowest reconstruction error, with an RMSE of 0.294 GeV. Under matched-data conditions with only 1,500 training events, the QLSTM improves on the classical LSTM by 52.7% and also surpasses an LSTM trained on the full set. These observations indicate that longitudinal representations are central to calorimeter energy reconstruction and give preliminary evidence that hybrid quantum-classical sequence models can be more sample-efficient for regression in high-energy physics.

We compare classical and quantum-enhanced models for incident positron energy reconstruction on the CaloGAN dataset, a public benchmark of 100,000 simulated electromagnetic shower events spanning 1 to 100 GeV. Eight architectures, namely SVR, ANN, CNN and LSTM together with their quantum counterparts, are trained on three calorimeter representations: engineered physical features, calorimeter images, and longitudinal shower sequences. Models that follow the longitudinal development of the shower reach the highest accuracy, which points to the value of physically informed representations. The hybrid QLSTM gives the lowest reconstruction error, with an RMSE of 0.294 GeV. Under matched-data conditions with only 1,500 training events, the QLSTM improves on the classical LSTM by 52.7% and also surpasses an LSTM trained on the full set. These observations indicate that longitudinal representations are central to calorimeter energy reconstruction and give preliminary evidence that hybrid quantum-classical sequence models can be more sample-efficient for regression in high-energy physics.

items.title: Enumerating Posterior-Supported Priors: First-Order Error of Finite-Integral Cross-Categorical Measurement Morphisms
items.originalTitle: Enumerating Posterior-Supported Priors: First-Order Error of Finite-Integral Cross-Categorical Measurement Morphisms
items.summary: arXiv:2611.17390v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: In generative modeling, standard measure theory adopts the a.e. convention, which legitimately ignores any error component carried by a null-support set: a single null element can hide out-of-domain error inside null support and never be explicitly accounted for. The contribution of this paper is not a new distributional distance, but rather a verifiable structure that writes down which underlying predicate supports a high-level object, when it is invertible, and at which layer the error resides, from which we propose the enumerating posterior-supported prior framework. The framework operates on a three-layer categorical chain Quot->MorTop->Set: the first two layers posit no point elements and take binary-predicate quotient partitions as objects; the replica-index counting measure successively discriminates one-to-many collections into injections, lifting object collection from surjection to a quotient-layer bijection; the mutual exclusion of preimages in the shared measure space is resolved by an invertible MPT. Four results consolidate into Thm. 7: binary quotient-partition meta-categorical objects support the set categorical functional along categorical support via measure descent--recovery, enumerating the morphism itself rather than its preimage and object; their multiplicity is normalized through replica-index injection and accounted as an explicitly first-order error. The contribution of this paper is a transformation from nontrivial-input construction -> engineering-computable first-order output: the binary quotient-partition meta-categorical objects, supported via categorical support measure descent--recovery, constitute a substantive nontrivial input---precisely because they lift the out-of-domain error that hid inside null support into a first-order falsifiable coefficient mu_err, a finitely obtainable finite integral first-order error.

items.title: Can LLMs Write Backdoors? An Empirical Security Study of Weight-Space Programming [ * ] [ ⬢ ]
items.originalTitle: Can LLMs Write Backdoors? An Empirical Security Study of Weight-Space Programming
items.summary: arXiv:2611.17395v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Recent advances in weight-space programming (WSP) have demonstrated that large language models (LLMs) can directly inspect and modify neural network weights without conventional gradient-based training. While this capability opens new possibilities for model improvement, it also raises an important security question: Can LLMs exploit weight-space programming to inject backdoors into neural networks? To answer this question, we present an empirical security study of LLM-driven weight-space programming for backdoor injection. Specifically, we investigate whether general-purpose LLMs can directly modify the weights of target models according to natural-language instructions, without accessing task-specific data, performing forward passes, or computing gradients. We evaluate five LLMs as weight editors across three target architectures: an MLP on MNIST, ResNet-18 on CIFAR-10, and Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct on AG News. Our experiments reveal three key findings. First, LLM-driven weight editing can successfully inject backdoors across different architectures while largely preserving clean performance. Second, successful attacks can require remarkably few parameter modifications, including only six parameters for the MLP and 0.02% of the weights for a fine-tuned Qwen model. Third, editing capabilities vary substantially across LLMs and target architectures: although all five LLMs successfully backdoor the MLP, only GPT-6 Astra succeeds across all three targets. These findings highlight an emerging security risk of weight-space programming and underscore the importance of safeguarding LLM-driven weight editing.

items.title: WETW: Learning Pair-Specific Weighted Euclidean Distances for Efficient DTW Search [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: WETW: Learning Pair-Specific Weighted Euclidean Distances for Efficient DTW Search
items.summary: arXiv:2611.17412v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Dynamic Time Warping (DTW) is the standard distance for similarity search over time series that are misaligned in time, but its cost is quadratic in the series length and lower bounds often prune few candidates, so search over large collections of long series is slow. Learned approximations embed the series to make comparisons cheap, yet compare every pair with the same fixed rule, usually the Euclidean distance, although DTW aligns each pair differently. We observe that, once a pair is aligned, DTW is a Euclidean distance over coordinates selected for that pair. Building on this view, we propose Weighted Euclidean Time Warping (WETW), a learned distance that adapts the comparison of fixed-length embeddings to each pair. A small symmetric network predicts one weight per embedding di- mension and pair without computing an alignment, which halves the error of the best static distance on the same embeddings. The embeddings come from the Weighted Euclidean SEries Encoder (WESEE), whose multi-scale Temporal Feature Extractor keeps the timing information that global pooling removes and raises recall@1 from 0.90 to 0.95, although WETW works with any encoder. We also show that fitting DTW distances is not enough for search, as regression alone misorders the closest neighbours, and that ranking regularization raises recall@1 from 0.79 to 0.95. Our filter-and-verify pipeline, WETW-FV, uses WETW to build a shortlist and exact DTW to check it, so the search is approximate but every returned distance is exact. Over eight datasets, WETW-FV is 11.4x faster than the fastest exact method among the UCR Suite, lower bounds and MESSI-DTW, at a mean recall@10 of 0.93, while the best learned baseline reaches 0.59 at the same speed. On 48K-point series, WETW- FV remains 40x faster than the UCR Suite at a recall@10 of 0.91.

items.title: Interpreting Coding Agents Through Their Behavioral Trajectories [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Interpreting Coding Agents Through Their Behavioral Trajectories
items.summary: arXiv:2611.17440v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Standard coding-agent benchmarks primarily evaluate binary task success, treating execution as a black box and obscuring the behaviors that produce those outcomes. We analyze a large corpus of 143,209 execution trajectories from 125 agent configurations spanning 117 unique models. To enable comparisons across heterogeneous agent interfaces, we develop a rule-based parser that maps raw execution traces to high-level actions such as repository search, file editing, and test execution, and audit its predictions against a six-model consensus reference on 500 events. We find that agents with similar solve rates can nevertheless differ substantially in how they explore, modify and verify code. Moreover, without using task outcomes, token counts, or tool names as features, aggregate behavioral profiles retrieve the corresponding agent stack across disjoint repository sets and programming languages, although task composition is not fully controlled in the cross-repository setting. Through analyses of frontier models and agent scaffolds, we further show that scaffold choice and reasoning effort systematically shift agents' search, editing, and testing behavior. We release the deterministic parser together with the full annotation and analysis pipeline alongside an annotated trajectory subset.
